WEEK 3 — RULES OF INFERENCE
1. RULES OF INFERENCE
Definition
Rules of inference are fundamental principles used in logic to draw valid conclusions from given premises.
These rules help ensure that logical arguments are structured in a way that preserves the truth of the premises.

pages.source: User-provided exact content — Rules of Inference — page 3
pages.text:
2. ARGUMENT
Definition
An argument is a structured series of statements or propositions where:
	One or more statements, known as premises, are presented as evidence or reasons.
	These premises support or justify another statement, known as the conclusion.
Basic structure
Premises → Conclusion

pages.source: User-provided exact content — Rules of Inference — page 4
pages.text:
3. TWO PARTS OF AN ARGUMENT
An argument consists of two main parts:
Premise
A premise is a statement or proposition presented as evidence or a reason.
Premises are intended to provide support for the conclusion.
Conclusion
The conclusion is the statement that the argument is trying to establish or prove.
The conclusion is the main point or claim of the argument.

pages.source: User-provided exact content — Rules of Inference — page 5
pages.text:
4. ARGUMENT EXAMPLE
The PPT gives the following argument:
Premise 1
All birds have wings
Premise 2
A parrot is a bird
Conclusion
Therefore, parrot has a wing.
The first two statements are the premises, while the final statement is the conclusion.

pages.source: User-provided exact content — Rules of Inference — page 6
pages.text:
5. MODUS PONENS
Definition
Modus Ponens (MP)
If P implies Q, and P is true, then Q must be true.
Formal Form
p ⇒ q
p
∴ q
Example
p: It’s raining.
q: The ground is wet.
Premise
If it’s raining, then the ground is wet.
Premise
It is raining.
Conclusion
∴ The ground is wet.
Structure
If:
	p ⇒ q
	p is true
Then:
	q must be true.

pages.source: User-provided exact content — Rules of Inference — page 7
pages.text:
6. MODUS TOLLENS
Definition
Modus Tollens (MT)
If P implies Q, and Q is false, then P must be false.
Formal Form
p ⇒ q
¬q
∴ ¬p
Example
p: It’s raining.
q: The ground is wet.
Premise
If it’s raining, then the ground is wet.
Premise
The ground is not wet.
Conclusion
∴ It is not raining.
Structure
If:
	p ⇒ q
	¬q
Then:
	¬p

pages.source: User-provided exact content — Rules of Inference — page 8
pages.text:
7. HYPOTHETICAL SYLLOGISM
Definition
Hypothetical Syllogism (HS)
If P implies Q, and Q implies R, then P implies R.
Formal Form
p ⇒ q
q ⇒ r
∴ p ⇒ r
Example
p: It’s raining.
q: The ground is wet.
r: The grass is slippery.
Premise 1
If it is raining, then the ground is wet.
Premise 2
If the ground is wet, then the grass is slippery.
Conclusion
∴ Therefore, it is raining, then the grass is slippery.

pages.source: User-provided exact content — Rules of Inference — page 9
pages.text:
Structure
If:
p ⇒ q
and:
q ⇒ r
then:
p ⇒ r

pages.source: User-provided exact content — Rules of Inference — page 10
pages.text:
8. DISJUNCTIVE SYLLOGISM
Definition
Disjunctive Syllogism (DS)
If either P or Q is true, and P is false, then Q must be true.
Formal Form
p ∨ q
¬p
∴ q
Example
p: I will make tea.
q: I will read a book.
Premise
I will make tea or read a book.
Premise
I will not make tea.
Conclusion
∴ Therefore, I will read a book.

pages.source: User-provided exact content — Rules of Inference — page 11
pages.text:
9. CONSTRUCTIVE DILEMMA
Definition
Constructive Dilemma (CD)
If P implies Q, and R implies S, and P or R is true, then Q or S is true.
Formal Form
The PPT presents:
(p ⇒ q) ^ (r ⇒ s)
p ∨ r
q ∨ s
Variables
p: Sara will wake up early.
q: Sara will exercise.
r: Lee will stay up late.
s: Lee will drink coffee.
Premise 1
If Sara will wake up early, then she will exercise AND If Lee will stay up late, then he will drink coffee.
Premise 2
Either Sara woke up early, or Lee stayed up late.
Conclusion
Therefore, Sara will either exercise or Lee will drink coffee.

pages.source: User-provided exact content — Rules of Inference — page 12
pages.text:
10. SIMPLIFICATION
Definition
Simplification (SIMP)
If P ∧ Q is true, then both P and Q are true.
Formal Form
p ^ q
∴ p
Example
The sky is blue and the grass is green.
Therefore:
∴ Therefore, the sky is blue.
Variables
p: Sky is blue
q: Grass is green
Structure
From:
p ∧ q
we can infer:
p
The same principle can also be used to infer:
q

pages.source: User-provided exact content — Rules of Inference — page 13
pages.text:
11. CONJUNCTION
Definition
Conjunction (CONJ)
If both P and Q are true, then P is true, and Q is true.
Formal Form
p
q
∴ p ^ q
Example
p: Juan is drinking coffee.
q: Juan reading a book.
Conclusion
∴ Therefore, Juan is drinking coffee AND reading a book
Structure
If:
	p is true
	q is true
Then:
p ∧ q
is true.

pages.source: User-provided exact content — Rules of Inference — page 14
pages.text:
12. ADDITION
Definition
Addition (ADD)
If P is true, then P or any other statement is true.
Formal Form
p
∴ p ∨ q
Example
Premise 1
It is sunny.
Conclusion
∴ Therefore, either it’s sunny or cloudy.
Structure
From:
p
we can infer:
p ∨ q

pages.source: User-provided exact content — Rules of Inference — page 15
pages.text:
13. DOUBLE NEGATION
Definition
The Double Negation (DN) rule allows us to simplify expressions by removing double negations without altering the meaning or truth value of the proposition.
Formal Form
p ↔ ¬ ¬ p
Example
Premise 1: DJ attended the class.
Same as:
DJ attended the class if and only if he did not, not attend class.
So:
DJ attended the class.
Important statement
Not not p is just p

pages.source: User-provided exact content — Rules of Inference — page 16
pages.text:
14. TAUTOLOGY
Definition
Tautology (TAU)
If P is a tautology, then P can be asserted as true without needing any premises.
Expressions
p ↔ (p ∨ p)
p ↔ (p ^ p)
Example
Premise: I will go to school.
I will go to school if and only if I will go to school OR I will go to school.
I will go to school if and only if I will go to school AND I will go to school.
Conclusion
I will go to school.
15. DE MORGAN'S RULE
Definition
De Morgan's Rule (DM) in logic is a pair of rules that describe how to negate:
	Conjunctions
	Disjunctions
There are two aspects of De Morgan's Rule:
	Negation of Conjunction (DM1)
	Negation of Disjunction (DM2)

pages.source: User-provided exact content — Rules of Inference — page 17
pages.text:
15.1 NEGATION OF CONJUNCTION — DM1
The negation of a conjunction is logically equivalent to the disjunction of the negations of its components.
Formula
¬ (p ^ q) ⇒ (¬p ∨ ¬q)
Meaning
When a conjunction is negated:
¬(p ∧ q)
it becomes:
¬p ∨ ¬q
The conjunction AND changes to OR, and each proposition is negated.

pages.source: User-provided exact content — Rules of Inference — page 18
pages.text:
15.2 NEGATION OF DISJUNCTION — DM2
The negation of a disjunction is logically equivalent to the conjunction of the negations of its components.
Formula
¬ (p ∨ q) ⇒ (¬p ^ ¬q)
Meaning
When a disjunction is negated:
¬(p ∨ q)
it becomes:
¬p ∧ ¬q
The disjunction OR changes to AND, and each proposition is negated.

pages.source: User-provided exact content — Rules of Inference — page 19
pages.text:
16. COMMUTATIVITY
Definition
The Commutativity (Com) property in logic refers to the ability to interchange the order of operands in a binary operation without changing the result.
In propositional logic, the Commutativity property applies to:
	Conjunction (∧)
	Disjunction (∨)
Formula shown in the PPT
p ∨ (q ∨ r) ↔ (q ∨ r) ∨ p
Core idea
The order of the operands can be changed without changing the result.

pages.source: User-provided exact content — Rules of Inference — page 20
pages.text:
17. ASSOCIATIVITY
Definition
The Associativity (Assoc) property in logic refers to the ability to group operands in a binary operation without changing the result.
In propositional logic, the Associativity property applies to:
	Conjunction (∧)
	Disjunction (∨)
The PPT identifies:
	Associativity of Conjunction (Assoc ∧)
	Associativity of Disjunction (Assoc ∨)

pages.source: User-provided exact content — Rules of Inference — page 21
pages.text:
17.1 Associativity of Conjunction
When multiple propositions are connected by conjunction, the result is the same regardless of how they are grouped.
Formula
[ p ^ (q ^ r) ] ↔ [ (p ^ q) ^ r ]
Core idea
The grouping can change:
p ∧ (q ∧ r)
to:
(p ∧ q) ∧ r
without changing the result.

pages.source: User-provided exact content — Rules of Inference — page 22
pages.text:
17.2 Associativity of Disjunction
When multiple propositions are connected by disjunction, the result is the same regardless of how they are grouped.
Formula
[ p ∨ (q ∨ r) ] ↔ [ (p ∨ q) ∨ r ]

pages.source: User-provided exact content — Rules of Inference — page 23
pages.text:
18. DISTRIBUTION
Definition
The Distribution (DIST) property in logic refers to the relationship between conjunction (∧) and disjunction (∨) operations.
It states how one operation distributes over the other.
The PPT identifies two forms:
	Distribution of Disjunction over Conjunction (DIST ∨/∧)
	Distribution of Conjunction over Disjunction (DIST ∧/∨)

pages.source: User-provided exact content — Rules of Inference — page 24
pages.text:
18.1 Distribution of Disjunction over Conjunction
Formula
[ p ∨ (q ^ r) ] ↔ [ (p ∨ q) ^ (p ∨ r) ]
Explanation
This means that disjunction distributes over conjunction, allowing us to expand a disjunction of a conjunction into a conjunction of disjunctions.
Transformation
p ∨ (q ∧ r)
becomes:
(p ∨ q) ∧ (p ∨ r)

pages.source: User-provided exact content — Rules of Inference — page 25
pages.text:
18.2 Distribution of Conjunction over Disjunction
Formula
[ p ^ (q ∨ r) ] ↔ [ (p ^ q) ∨ (p ^ r) ]
Explanation
This means that conjunction distributes over disjunction, allowing us to expand a conjunction of a disjunction into a disjunction of conjunctions.
Transformation
p ∧ (q ∨ r)
becomes:
(p ∧ q) ∨ (p ∧ r)

pages.source: User-provided exact content — Rules of Inference — page 26
pages.text:
19. TRANSPOSITION
Definition
Transposition (TRANS) is a rule of inference in logic that involves switching the positions of the antecedent and consequent of a conditional statement, as long as both are negated.
Formula
(p ⇒ q) ↔ (¬q ⇒ ¬p)
Structure
Original:
p ⇒ q
Transposed:
¬q ⇒ ¬p
The antecedent and consequent switch positions, and both are negated.

pages.source: User-provided exact content — Rules of Inference — page 27
pages.text:
20. MATERIAL IMPLICATION
Definition / Rule
Material Implication (IMPL)
The PPT states:
If P is false, then P→Q is considered true, regardless of the truth value of Q.
Formula
(p ⇒ q) ↔ (¬p ∨ q)
Transformation
A conditional:
p ⇒ q
can be expressed as:
¬p ∨ q

pages.source: User-provided exact content — Rules of Inference — page 28
pages.text:
21. MATERIAL EQUIVALENCE
Definition / Rule
Material Equivalence (EQUIV)
The PPT states:
If P and Q are materially equivalent, then P implies Q and Q implies P.
Formula shown in the PPT
(p ⇒ q) ↔ [(p ⇒ q) ^ (q ⇒ p)]
Core idea
Material equivalence involves implications in both directions:
p ⇒ q
and:
q ⇒ p

pages.source: User-provided exact content — Rules of Inference — page 29
pages.text:
22. EXPORTATION
Definition
Exportation (EXP)
The Exportation rule states that if we have a nested implication of the form:
P → (Q → R)
we can transform it into an equivalent form using conjunctions and implications.
Formula
[(p ^ q) ⇒ r] ↔ [p ⇒ (q ⇒ r)]
Transformation
One equivalent form is:
(p ∧ q) ⇒ r
The other equivalent form is:
p ⇒ (q ⇒ r)
